opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think money is mostly a tool for freedom. It's not something I think about as a goal in itself. What it really buys you is the ability to choose what you work on, and who you work with, without being forced into decisions just to survive.

For someone like me who works in research and building systems, that freedom matters a lot. The most exciting problems often don't have an obvious payoff at first. If you're always worried about the next paycheck, it's very hard to take the risk of spending a year or two on something that might not work. So having enough financial security lets you be patient and a bit stubborn about the things you believe in.

Beyond a certain point, though, I don't think more money changes your day-to-day happiness much. What really motivates me is seeing something we built actually get used, like when people pick up a piece of open-source software and run their models faster with it, or when a student tells me they learned something from our work. That kind of impact feels much more meaningful than a number in a bank account.

Money also gives you the ability to support other people: your family, or young researchers and engineers who are just starting out and need resources to pursue their ideas. So I'd say it's a means to freedom, to impact, and to taking care of the people around you, but not the end goal.

r001.rationale: She describes money as practically useful for financial security, taking risks, and supporting others, while saying it is not a goal or end in itself.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention confidence from having a fallback to finance her company if external fundraising fails.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think about money mostly as a kind of freedom, and specifically freedom from having to think about money. When I was a PhD student, money meant being able to not worry about rent in the Bay Area, which, as anyone who has lived there knows, is not a small thing. Later, when I was building open-source projects like SGLang, money meant something different: it was whether we could get enough GPUs to run experiments, whether we could keep a team together, whether the thing we were building could survive long enough to matter.

So I don't think of money as a goal in itself. I've never been very good at optimizing for it directly. But I've come to respect it as a resource, the same way you respect compute or time. It buys you the ability to say no to things you don't want to do, and to say yes to the risky thing, like leaving a comfortable position to go build something from scratch. That optionality is what I value most.

And there's one more piece, which is that money is a signal. When a company or a customer is willing to pay for what you've built, that tells you it's actually useful to someone, not just interesting to you. For a researcher that feedback loop is surprisingly important, because in academia it's easy to spend years on something that's elegant but that nobody needs. So I'd say money means freedom, it means fuel, and it means a reality check. In that order.

r001.rationale: The response describes practical uses for money, such as rent and funding GPUs and a team, while saying it is not a goal he optimizes for and identifying optionality as what he values most.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that personal wealth would provide a fallback to finance the company if external fundraising failed.

astra-6.text: To me, money means having choices. It gives you some security and the freedom to decide how you spend your time, what you want to work on, and when you can say no. I think the important question is what you want money to make possible. Otherwise, it’s easy to keep chasing a bigger number without knowing what would ever feel like enough.

r001.rationale: The response describes money as providing choices and security, but does not distinguish Ying Sheng’s practical need for money from its importance as a personal priority.

r002.rationale: It mentions security and the freedom to say no, but does not say her personal wealth could fund her company if external fundraising fails.
